\chapter{One to Five, and the Words English Already Says}
\label{ch:fa-count-five}
\hlchaptermodality{16}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say, hear and recognise the Persian numbers one to five, write the one of them made only of letters I have been taught, and name the English cousin of each.}

Five numbers, five Indo-European roots and five everyday English cousins — retrieved shuffled rather than recited, with the one writable form written.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[yek]{\fa{یک} — one, and the first number this book has ever taught}

\label{lesson:FA-C16-yek}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\fa{سلام}} and \textbf{\fa{نان}} off the page, without the romanization. Nine letters, and the words they finish.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{یک}} — \emph{yek} — \textbf{one}
\end{quote}

Fifteen chapters of names, verbs, kinship, the body and the sky, and not one number. That has a cost the book has been carrying quietly: no age, no price, no telephone number, no quantity, no time of day. It starts being paid here.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{یک}} continues Middle Persian \textbf{yak}, from Proto-Iranian *\emph{Haywah} and Indo-Iranian *\emph{Háywas}, ultimately Indo-European *\emph{óywos}, \textquotedblleft{}one.\textquotedblright{}

That root did not stay in Iran. Sanskrit \emph{eka}, Ancient Greek \emph{oios}, Latin \textbf{ūnus}, French \textbf{un}, German \textbf{ein} and English \textbf{one} are all the same word, worn down differently. Of the ten numbers this slice teaches, nine have a cousin an English speaker already says every day — which makes the count the cheapest vocabulary in the whole book, not the most expensive.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{yek} — one
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{yek} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{óywos} $\to$ English \textbf{one}, Latin \textbf{ūnus}, Sanskrit \textbf{eka}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\fa{یک}} mean? (\textbf{One}.) Which everyday English word is the same root? (\textbf{One}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%DB\%8C\%DA\%A9}{Wiktionary: \fa{یک}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[do]{\fa{دو} — two, and a letter doing its third job}

\label{lesson:FA-C16-do}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{yek}, and the English word that is the same root.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{دو}} — \emph{do} — \textbf{two}
\end{quote}

Two letters. The second is \textbf{\fa{و}}, the hard-working letter from the script chapter that can be \emph{v}, \emph{u} or \emph{o}; here it is \textbf{o}, and the word tells you so.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{دو}} continues Middle Persian \textbf{dō}, from Proto-Iranian *\emph{duwā}, from Indo-European *\emph{dwoh}, \textquotedblleft{}two.\textquotedblright{} English \textbf{two}, Latin \textbf{duo}, Greek \textbf{dýo} and Sanskrit \textbf{dvá} are the same word.

Say \emph{do} and \emph{two} one after the other. Nothing has to be learned there; it has to be recognised.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{do} — two
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{do} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{dwoh} $\to$ English \textbf{two}, Latin \textbf{duo}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{yek, do}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \fa{و}'s three jobs is it doing in \textbf{\fa{دو}}? (\textbf{o}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AF\%D9\%88}{Wiktionary: \fa{دو}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[se]{\fa{سه} — three, and the first number the hand can make}

\label{lesson:FA-C16-se}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{yek}, \textbf{do}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{سه}} — \emph{se} — \textbf{three}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\fa{س}} and \textbf{\fa{ه}}. Both were taught in the script chapter, so this is the first number in the book you can write as well as say. Of the twelve numbers this slice covers, exactly two are in that position — the other is nine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{سه}} continues Middle Persian \textbf{sē}, from Indo-European *\emph{tréyes}, \textquotedblleft{}three.\textquotedblright{} English \textbf{three}, Latin \textbf{trēs}, Greek \textbf{treîs} and Sanskrit \textbf{tri} are the same word.

The Persian form looks further away than \emph{do} did, and it is: the initial consonant and the \emph{r} have both gone. Hearing \emph{se} as \emph{three} takes a moment where hearing \emph{do} as \emph{two} took none — that is worth noticing now, because the next two numbers are further still.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{se} — three
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{se} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{tréyes} $\to$ English \textbf{three}, Latin \textbf{trēs}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\fa{سه}} — sin, then he. Right to left.
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{yek, do, se}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two numbers can this book write so far? (\textbf{\fa{سه}} and, later, \textbf{\fa{نه}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%B3\%D9\%87}{Wiktionary: \fa{سه}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chahâr]{\fa{چهار} — four, and one consonant taking three different paths}

\label{lesson:FA-C16-chahar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{se} and its English cousin, then \textbf{do}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{چهار}} — \emph{chahâr} — \textbf{four}
\end{quote}

Two syllables, and the long \textbf{â} of \textbf{\fa{باران}} in the second.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{چهار}} continues Old Persian \textbf{chathwar}, from Indo-European *\emph{k\textsuperscript{w}etwóres}, \textquotedblleft{}four.\textquotedblright{}

That opening *\emph{k\textsuperscript{w}} is the interesting part, because three languages did three different things with it. Latin kept it whole: \textbf{quattuor}. English lost the lip-rounding and then the \emph{k} itself softened to \emph{f}: \textbf{four}. Persian pushed it forward to a \textbf{ch}. One sound, three descendants, and the numbers still line up.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{chahâr} — four
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{chahâr} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{k\textsuperscript{w}etwóres} $\to$ Latin \textbf{quattuor}, English \textbf{four}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{yek, do, se, chahâr}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which language kept the original \textbf{kw} whole? (\textbf{Latin}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%DA\%86\%D9\%87\%D8\%A7\%D8\%B1}{Wiktionary: \fa{چهار}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[panj]{\fa{پنج} — five, and the word you have already met on a map}

\label{lesson:FA-C16-panj}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{chahâr}, and what three languages did with its first sound.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{پنج}} — \emph{panj} — \textbf{five}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\fa{پ}} is Persian's own letter, one of the four the alphabet added for sounds Arabic does not have.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{پنج}} continues Middle Persian \textbf{panj}, from Indo-European *\emph{pénk\textsuperscript{w}e}, \textquotedblleft{}five.\textquotedblright{} Greek \textbf{pénte}, Latin \textbf{quīnque} and English \textbf{five} are the same word.

This one an English speaker has probably already met without knowing it. \textbf{Punjab} is \emph{panj} + \emph{âb}, \textquotedblleft{}five waters\textquotedblright{} — the land of the five rivers. So is the fruit drink \textbf{punch}, named for its five ingredients. The number was in the language before the lesson was.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{panj} — five
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{panj} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{pénk\textsuperscript{w}e} $\to$ Greek \textbf{pénte}, Latin \textbf{quīnque}, English \textbf{five}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{yek, do, se, chahâr, panj} — the whole first five
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \textbf{panj} in \textbf{Punjab} mean? (\textbf{Five}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%BE\%D9\%86\%D8\%AC}{Wiktionary: \fa{پنج}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — one to five, out of order}

\label{lesson:FA-C16-practice}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{panj}, then \textbf{yek}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A run learned forwards is a rhyme. Break it four ways.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Hear each of the five named singly and out of order, and say what it is.
  \item Count backwards from \textbf{panj} to \textbf{yek}.
  \item Read the five printed shuffled — \textbf{\fa{پنج،} \fa{یک،} \fa{چهار،} \fa{سه،} \fa{دو}} — and say each.
  \item Write \textbf{\fa{سه}}, the one of the five whose letters are already yours.
\end{enumerate}

Then say each number's English cousin: \textbf{one, two, three, four, five}. Every one of the five has one, and that is not a coincidence — it is the same set of words, five thousand years apart.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
